person.description: A person whose U.S. citizenship status under the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause is at issue in the debate.

born_in_us.description: Recorded as born on U.S. soil. Both sides of the debate accept this predicate and its extension without dispute.

us_citizen.description: Recorded as a U.S. citizen under the Citizenship Clause reading at issue. Both sides accept the predicate; they dispute its extension for specific people because they dispute the extension of subject_to_jurisdiction.

subject_to_jurisdiction.description: Recorded as satisfying 'subject to the jurisdiction thereof' (14th Amendment, Citizenship Clause). THIS IS THE CONTESTED PREDICATE: both sides use the same word 'jurisdiction' and accept the same syntactic role for it in the Citizenship Clause, but assign it different extensions. Krikorian/Cooper read it as complete, exclusive political allegiance (owing no allegiance to a foreign sovereign); Mayes/Newman read it as being present in U.S. territory and bound by / enforceable under U.S. law. See claim-graph.md.

has_noncitizen_domiciled_parent.description: Recorded as having at least one parent who is a non-citizen permanently domiciled/residing in the U.S. but legally ineligible for naturalization (the parental profile in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, 1898). Both sides accept Wong Kim Ark's outcome for this profile.

has_noncitizen_undocumented_parent.description: Recorded as having at least one parent who is a non-citizen present in the U.S. without legal immigration status. This is the profile the 'end birthright citizenship' side argues falls outside subject_to_jurisdiction, and the 'keep it' side argues falls inside it.

has_noncitizen_temporary_parent.description: Recorded as having at least one parent who is a non-citizen present in the U.S. only temporarily (tourist, student, or other non-immigrant visa) -- the 'birth tourism' profile Krikorian raises.

child.description: A representative child born in the United States, used to test the debate's central syllogism concretely (the debate's own paradigm example, not a real individual).
